name: PE / Windows executable
explanation: Every Windows Portable Executable (PE) binary begins with the two-byte 'MZ' signature (0x4D 0x5A) which is the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER.e_magic field, named after Mark Zbikowski. The bytes that follow form the rest of the DOS stub plus a 4-byte offset at file offset 0x3C (e_lfanew) that points to the IMAGE_NT_HEADERS where the actual PE header lives. So when you see 'MZ' at offset 0 you are looking at .exe, .dll, .sys, .efi, .scr, or any other Windows-loadable image; the variant comes from the PE header that the e_lfanew offset reveals.

name: ELF / Unix-like executable
explanation: Linux, BSD, and Solaris executables begin with the four-byte ELF magic (0x7F followed by 'ELF'). Byte 4 says 32-bit (0x01) or 64-bit (0x02); byte 5 is endianness (0x01 little, 0x02 big); byte 6 is ELF version (always 0x01 today); byte 7 is OS ABI. After a 16-byte e_ident block, e_type at offset 16 says executable (ET_EXEC = 0x02), shared object (ET_DYN = 0x03), relocatable (ET_REL = 0x01), or core (ET_CORE = 0x04). Modern PIE binaries are ET_DYN even though they are 'executables' from the user perspective; check the INTERP segment to disambiguate.

name: Mach-O 64-bit (macOS executable)
explanation: macOS 64-bit Mach-O binaries begin with the magic 0xFEEDFACF in big-endian order, which on disk is 'CF FA ED FE' little-endian. The 32-bit variant uses 0xFEEDFACE / 'CE FA ED FE'. The bytes that follow encode CPU type (e.g. 0x01000007 = x86_64, 0x0100000C = ARM64), CPU subtype, file type (MH_EXECUTE = 0x02, MH_DYLIB = 0x06, MH_BUNDLE = 0x08), number of load commands, and load command size. Universal / fat binaries that bundle multiple architectures begin with 0xCAFEBABE ('CA FE BA BE') which is also Java class-file magic, so context matters.

name: ZIP / Office Open XML / JAR / APK
explanation: The ZIP format starts with 'PK' followed by a 2-byte record type (0x0304 = local file header, 0x0102 = central directory, 0x0506 = end-of-central-directory). Modern Microsoft Office files (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) are ZIP containers whose first entry is the [Content_Types].xml part; Java JARs and Android APKs are also ZIPs. So 'PK 03 04' alone says 'this is a ZIP container' but does not say which kind. Look at the path of the first inner entry, or look for 'word/' (DOCX), 'xl/' (XLSX), 'META-INF/MANIFEST.MF' (JAR), 'AndroidManifest.xml' (APK).

name: PDF document
explanation: PDFs begin with '%PDF-' followed by a version string ('1.4', '1.7', '2.0'). The %PDF- header may not literally be at offset 0 if the file has a UTF-8 BOM or other prefix bytes, but most parsers tolerate up to 1024 bytes of leading garbage by spec. PDFs of interest in cybersec usually carry malicious JavaScript via the /JavaScript or /JS keys in the object dictionary, embedded files via /EmbeddedFile, or launch actions via /Launch. The file ends with '%%EOF' and may have multiple trailers due to incremental updates; look for '%PDF-' near the start AND '%%EOF' near the end to confirm structure.

name: OLE2 compound document (legacy Office, MSI)
hex_at_offset_0: D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1
explanation: The OLE2 / Compound File Binary format magic is 0xD0CF11E0A1B11AE1 (a binary palindrome around 0xE0). It is the container format for legacy Office (.doc, .xls, .ppt before 2007), Microsoft Installer packages (.msi), Windows shortcut files (.lnk, sometimes), and several other Microsoft formats. From an attacker's perspective the OLE2 container is interesting because it can carry VBA macros, OLE-embedded payloads, and exploit shellcode in malformed streams. Distinguishing the inner format requires reading the root entry's CLSID and the named streams.

name: PNG image
explanation: PNG starts with an 8-byte signature: 0x89 (high-bit set, breaks 7-bit text systems), 'PNG' (the format), CRLF (line-ending sanity check), 0x1A (DOS EOF), LF. After the signature the file is a chain of length-tag-data-CRC chunks; the first chunk is always IHDR (header). PNGs are interesting in cybersec because of steganography (LSB-encoded data in pixel bytes), 'polyglot' files that are both a PNG and a ZIP, and historical bugs in libpng allowing memory disclosure. Look for unusually large IDAT chunks or text chunks (tEXt, iTXt) with binary-looking content for steganography.

name: UPX-packed binary signature
explanation: UPX is the most common open-source PE / ELF / Mach-O packer. A UPX-packed binary keeps its original PE / ELF header but the section table contains sections named 'UPX0' (0x55 0x50 0x58 0x30, an empty section that will hold the unpacked code), 'UPX1' (the packed body), and 'UPX2' / '.rsrc' for resources. The 'UPX!' marker (0x55 0x50 0x58 0x21) appears later in the file as part of the UPX header structure that the unpacking stub reads at runtime. Detection: look at section names. False positive rate is near-zero because legitimate compilers do not emit sections named 'UPX0' / 'UPX1'.

name: Themida / VMProtect signs of obfuscation
longer_pattern: (typical Themida section: '.themida' or '.taggant'; VMProtect uses '.vmp0' / '.vmp1' / '.vmp2' section names)
explanation: Commercial protectors Themida (Oreans) and VMProtect leave specific named sections in the PE that survive unless the operator strips them. Themida-packed binaries typically contain '.themida' or '.taggant' sections; VMProtect uses '.vmp0', '.vmp1', '.vmp2'. They also produce extremely large entry-point dispatcher routines (10K+ instructions of branching and constant-folding obfuscation), high entropy in the code section (>7.0 bits per byte versus ~5.5 for normal compiled C++), and frequent CPUID / RDTSC / IsDebuggerPresent calls in the unpacker stub. Detection at offset 0 is fragile; reach for entropy + section name + import table patterns.

name: NOP sled (x86)
explanation: A sequence of 0x90 bytes is the x86 single-byte NOP instruction. Attackers prepend a NOP sled to shellcode to widen the landing zone for an imprecise return-address overwrite: as long as control flow lands anywhere in the sled, execution slides forward instruction-by-instruction until it hits the actual payload. Modern variants use 'pseudo-NOPs' that are non-90 instructions which still preserve the architectural state (e.g. 0x40 = inc eax, 0x48 = dec eax in 32-bit mode) to evade signature-based detection. Long runs of 0x90 in a buffer that is not normally code (a network packet payload, a file upload buffer) are a strong signal.

name: x64 function prologue
explanation: A canonical x86_64 function prologue: 0x55 (push rbp), 0x48 0x89 0xE5 (mov rbp, rsp), 0x48 0x83 0xEC 0x?? (sub rsp, N) where N is the local-variable stack size, then 0x48 0x89 0x7D 0xF8 (mov [rbp-8], rdi) which saves the first integer argument. Recognising this pattern by eye is fundamental to manual reversing: it tells you you are at a function entry, the local frame size is the byte that follows 'sub rsp', and the calling convention is System V AMD64 (rdi = arg1, rsi = arg2, rdx = arg3, rcx = arg4, r8 = arg5, r9 = arg6). Microsoft x64 passes args in rcx/rdx/r8/r9 instead.
examples: objdump -d output of a compiled C function

name: Linux x64 syscall pattern
explanation: On Linux x86_64, system calls are issued via the SYSCALL instruction (0x0F 0x05) after loading the syscall number into rax. Common patterns in shellcode: '48 31 C0 B0 3B' (xor rax,rax; mov al, 0x3B = execve), '48 31 FF' (xor rdi, rdi to zero out arg1), 'B8 01 00 00 00 0F 05' (mov eax, 1 = write, then syscall). Recognising 0x0F 0x05 in an unexpected location (a network buffer, a heap allocation that should hold data) is a strong signal that shellcode is present. Static analysis tools key on this; sandboxes hook the SYSCALL instruction in user-mode for instrumentation.

name: PE Optional Header Magic (PE32 vs PE32+)
explanation: Inside the IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER (which despite its name is mandatory for executable PEs), the first WORD is the Magic field: 0x010B for 32-bit images (PE32) and 0x020B for 64-bit images (PE32+). Note the byte order on disk is little-endian, so 0x010B appears as '0B 01' and 0x020B as '0B 02'. This field is the disambiguator between IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 and IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 layouts; the 64-bit variant is 16 bytes longer because BaseOfData is removed and ImageBase / SizeOfStackReserve / SizeOfStackCommit / SizeOfHeapReserve / SizeOfHeapCommit grow to 8 bytes each. A PE viewer that misreads this field corrupts every subsequent offset.
examples: the Magic field readable via Hex Workshop or HxD

name: PE Machine field (architecture)
explanation: The IMAGE_FILE_HEADER.Machine field at the start of the PE header (right after the 'PE\0\0' signature) declares the target architecture. Common values: 0x014C (IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_I386 = 32-bit x86), 0x8664 (AMD64 = 64-bit x86), 0xAA64 (ARM64), 0x01C4 (ARMNT = 32-bit ARM Thumb-2), 0x0200 (Itanium IA64, deprecated). Reading this field tells you which disassembler / debugger to attach. Attackers occasionally manipulate this field (or the corresponding ELF e_machine) to confuse static analysis tools that key on it for unpacker-arch selection.
examples: a 32-bit malware sample on a 64-bit host (run via WoW64)
ARM64 mobile malware compiled for newer Macs

name: Linux x64 execve('/bin/sh') shellcode
explanation: A compact 28-byte Linux x86_64 execve('/bin/sh', NULL, NULL) shellcode. Decoded: 'xor rax, rax' (zero rax), 'push rax' (push the null terminator that '/bin/sh\0' will reference), 'mov rbx, 0x0068732F6E69622F' (the string '/bin/sh' little-endian-encoded), 'push rbx', 'mov rdi, rsp' (rdi points at '/bin/sh'), 'xor rdx, rdx' (envp = NULL), 'xor rsi, rsi' (argv = NULL), 'mov al, 0x3B' (sys_execve number), 'syscall'. Recognising this exact byte string is one of the canonical IDS signatures for stage-2 shellcode landing in memory. Variants permute the register-zeroing instructions or use alphanumeric encoders to evade naive pattern matchers.
examples: a stage-1 dropper that executes after a stack overflow
